name: Administrative Justice Court
description: Iran’s Administrative Justice Court reviews specified complaints concerning public administration and challenges to administrative regulations. Its constitutional mandate places it within the judiciary, while legislation defines the boundaries of its jurisdiction.

seo.title: Administrative Justice Court in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran’s Administrative Justice Court, its constitutional mandate, administrative review functions, and the limits of the available evidence.

content.heading: A court for disputes about public administration
content.content:
The Administrative Justice Court, known in Persian as Divan-e Edalat-e Edari, provides a constitutionally established channel for complaints about public administration. Article 173 places it under the supervision of the head of the judiciary and leaves its jurisdiction, powers, and procedures to legislation. This institutional position matters: administrative review takes place within Iran’s judicial structure rather than through an authority outside it. [s1]

Article 170 supplies a related constitutional principle. Judges must decline to apply government regulations that conflict with the specified legal standards or exceed executive authority, and individuals may request their annulment through the Administrative Justice Court. Read together, these provisions distinguish reviewing administrative action from simply reconsidering the merits of a government policy. They establish legal responsibilities; they do not themselves demonstrate how consistently remedies work in practice. [s1]

content.heading: Individual decisions and general regulations
content.content:
The court’s legislation distinguishes complaints about particular administrative decisions from challenges to regulations of broader application. Article 10 covers specified decisions and actions of public bodies and their officials. It also provides for review of final decisions by designated administrative bodies, including tax commissions and labour-dispute boards, on grounds concerning violations of laws and regulations. Employment-rights complaints by covered public employees form another part of its remit. [s2]

A separate function belongs to the General Assembly, whose jurisdiction under Article 12 includes reviewing qualifying regulations. The distinction is consequential: a complaint about an individual administrative decision and a request to annul a generally applicable rule raise different questions and follow different statutory routes. The court also has internal arrangements for promoting consistent decisions. [s2]

content.heading: Authority and practical effectiveness
content.content:
The inspected consolidated law incorporates amendments dated 1402/02/10 in Iran’s Solar Hijri calendar. It addresses interim relief, enforcement, and circumstances in which the court can determine compensation connected with failures to perform specified legal duties. These provisions make older descriptions of the court potentially incomplete. [s2]

For an international reader, the essential distinction is between the existence of a review mechanism and evidence of effective redress. This account establishes elements of the legal framework. It does not establish typical waiting times, compliance with judgments, or the likelihood that a particular claimant will obtain relief.

name: State Organization for Registration of Deeds & Properties
description: The State Organization for Registration of Deeds and Properties has statutory responsibilities for Iran’s cadastre and cadastral ownership documents. Its registration remit also extends to industrial property, linking land records with a separate system for recording rights such as patents and trademarks.

seo.title: Iran’s State Organization for Registration of Deeds & Properties
seo.description: Explore the organization’s cadastral and industrial-property responsibilities, and distinguish statutory registration duties from verified implementation.

content.heading: Connecting legal records with identifiable property
content.content:
The State Organization for Registration of Deeds and Properties is named in Iran’s Comprehensive Cadastre Law as the body responsible for implementing cadastral work, issuing cadastral ownership documents, and establishing and operating the integrated information system described in that law. Its Persian name is Sazman-e Sabt-e Asnad va Amlak-e Keshvar. [s1]

A cadastre is more than a collection of maps. The law defines it as an organized record of land parcels that combines mapping with characteristics such as size, use, and registration or legal information. Cadastral work includes surveying, checking maps against conditions on the ground, adding descriptive and legal records, and updating the resulting information. This explains why a boundary drawing and an ownership document perform related but different functions. [s1]

content.heading: An extensive statutory ambition
content.content:
Adopted on 1393/11/12 in the Solar Hijri calendar, the cadastre law sets an extensive national scope. Article 3 requires the identification and stabilization of boundaries across public and private land and specified natural features, with information made usable through cadastral maps and ownership documents. This is a statutory obligation, not evidence that the intended coverage has been achieved. [s1]

The distinction is especially important when describing digital registration. A law can require an integrated information system without establishing that every historic record has been reconciled, every boundary dispute resolved, or every locality served equally. The inspected material supports an explanation of the system’s intended structure; it does not support a national completion percentage.

content.heading: Registration beyond land
content.content:
The organization also appears in Iran’s industrial-property framework. Article 134 of the 2024 Industrial Property Protection Act, in the inspected English translation, identifies it as the registration authority for matters including inventions, industrial designs, trademarks, and geographical indications. These are rights concerning creations, commercial identifiers, or product origin, rather than physical land boundaries. The article also assigns representation concerning industrial-property matters before the World Intellectual Property Organization and relevant convention unions. [s2]

These two areas should not be conflated. A cadastral ownership document and a trademark registration concern different objects and legal processes. Their institutional connection helps explain the breadth of the organization’s name, but an application’s registration does not by itself establish the organization’s overall effectiveness. A fuller account requires verified evidence about its other registration services and the implementation of recent property-law reforms.

name: Bar Associations
description: Iranian bar associations are professional institutions whose history is closely connected to struggles over lawyers’ independence and access to legal defence. Understanding them requires distinguishing their claim to professional self-government from judicial oversight and the separate judiciary-linked route into legal practice.

seo.title: Bar Associations and Lawyers’ Independence in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Discover the history of Iran’s bar associations, professional self-government, parallel licensing structures, and documented pressures on independent defence.

content.heading: Why professional independence matters
content.content:
A bar association is a professional institution for lawyers, rather than a court or a government ministry. In Iran, the question of who controls the profession has long shaped debates about the ability of lawyers to represent clients independently. The Iran Human Rights Documentation Center’s historical account connects the right to counsel with the institutional arrangements governing lawyers, their associations, and professional discipline. [s1]

The distinction is practical as well as constitutional. A formal entitlement to legal representation does not settle who may obtain a licence, who can stand for a professional association’s governing board, or who can remove a lawyer from practice. These arrangements affect the space in which defence lawyers work. UN special rapporteurs raised precisely these concerns in a communication to Iran’s government in 2021. [s2]

content.heading: The independence settlement and its later constraints
content.content:
The modern independence settlement is associated with Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddeq. The historical account inspected for this page dates the communication of the independence law to 1953 and its subsequent reaffirmation, with changes, to 1955. It describes the law as recognizing the bar’s separate legal personality and independence. Later political changes repeatedly altered the profession’s ability to govern itself. [s1]

This history helps explain why Iranian discussions of the bar often focus on independence rather than simply membership. Questions about board elections, licensing, and disciplinary jurisdiction concern the distribution of authority between professional institutions and the judiciary. A claim to independence in founding legislation therefore needs to be assessed alongside subsequent rules and documented practice. [s1][s2]

content.heading: More than one route into legal practice
content.content:
The International Bar Association’s Human Rights Institute and the Centre for Supporters of Human Rights describe a parallel judiciary-supervised body created under Article 187 of the Third Development Plan legislation. Its existence means that references to Iranian lawyers should not automatically be treated as references to members of the historically independent bar associations. The report interprets this parallel structure as a constraint on bar autonomy. That interpretation is the report’s assessment, rather than a neutral description of all lawyers’ individual conduct. [s3]

The same report, published in 2025, documents pressures on lawyers and bar institutions, including restrictive regulation and prosecutions. The earlier UN communication questioned judicial vetting of governing-board candidates and interference with professional regulation. These sources establish serious documented concerns, while differing in date and institutional perspective. [s2][s3]

content.heading: Reading institutional claims carefully
content.content: The central issue is the relationship between professional self-government and the conditions under which lawyers can act for clients. Historical legal recognition, present regulatory powers, and reported interference are separate kinds of evidence. The available research supports this distinction, but a complete contemporary directory of associations, licensing rules, and disciplinary procedures still requires further verification. [s1][s2][s3]
